rejection:
RECOMMENDATION: Reject. Confidence 4/5. Primary grounds: the three-part novelty claim is false as stated (all three parts have peer-reviewed or clearly prior precedent), the identification argument the paper needs does not exist and is not supplied, and the experimental protocol as described cannot separate the proposed causal machinery from extra inference compute.

=== 1. "First to formulate multi-turn human-LLM prompting as a longitudinal causal problem" is not first, and is not even first in a peer-reviewed venue ===

Three separate priorities defeat this.

(a) Prompt-as-treatment is published and peer-reviewed. Wang et al., AAAI-25 (Proc. AAAI 39(14):15212-15220, DOI 10.1609/aaai.v39i14.33669) states in its abstract that "the instructions are treated as the treatment." Frauen et al., "Causal methods for LLM development and evaluation" (arXiv:2605.25998, KDD 2026) states the prompt-as-treatment / outcome-as-reward framing outright, explicitly frames agentic systems as sequential decisions with causal estimands, and names doubly robust and orthogonal policy learning as the directly relevant tooling. A KDD 2026 position paper that announces the authors' own framing, sequential case included, is fatal to a "first to formulate" claim. The paper under review does not cite it.

(b) Longitudinal causal inference over text already exists. Nakamura and Imai, "GenAI Powered Dynamic Causal Inference with Unstructured Data" (arXiv:2605.07834) estimates effects of *sequences* of treatment features in unstructured text via a marginal structural model with a per-feature deconfounder and semiparametric CIs, and demonstrates position-dependent effects. Its companion, Imai and Nakamura (arXiv:2410.00903), supplies nonparametric ATE identification for text treatments with DML asymptotics and an explicit strategy for avoiding overlap violations. Any related-work section on multi-round text-as-treatment that omits these is not a survey, it is an omission.

(c) Causal analysis of multi-turn LLM history already exists. "What if LLMs Ate Their Words: Causal History Effects in Multi-Turn Interaction" (arXiv:2609.05882) performs step-level counterfactual interventions on assistant turns ("Neutralization," "Turn Surgery") over ~3000 conversations and establishes that specific assistant turns have selective downstream effects. The authors' framing is therefore motivated prior work, not their discovery.

=== 2. "Sequential blip/Q effects of language-valued interventions" is two off-the-shelf estimators plus the one hard part left undone ===

The estimators are not new. DeepBlip (arXiv:2511.14545, ICML 2026) is already a neural SNMM that learns all blip functions jointly under a Neyman-orthogonal loss. Javurek et al. (arXiv:2509.26429, ICLR 2026) already give a doubly robust, Neyman-orthogonal, quasi-oracle DRQ-learner for Q-functions from logged trajectories. If the paper's contribution is "apply these to text," then the contribution is exactly the step neither paper supports, and the paper must carry it. It does not.

Worse, invoking "blip/Q" as one object is a category error that suggests the estimand is unpinned. A blip is a contrast conditional on full history H_t, defined against a reference treatment level 0 (DeepBlip's gamma_{t,k} is explicitly a contrast against a_{t:t+k-1},0). A Q-function is a *level* under a fixed evaluation policy in a time-invariant MDP conditioning on S_t alone. These are different targets under different assumptions. Which is estimated? Two specific consequences:

- There is no canonical zero utterance. Silence, an empty prompt, and a neutral acknowledgement are all distinct actions that move the user's state. The blip decomposition is therefore choice-dependent and the reported g-estimates are artifacts of an arbitrary reference, with no sensitivity analysis offered.
- If the paper invokes Q, it inherits the Markov assumption on S_t, which assumes away precisely the time-varying confounding by conversation history that motivates the paper. The MDP conditioning set is a real strengthening relative to the longitudinal papers, not a convenience.

=== 3. The identification claim is unsupported, and the literature says so ===

There is, as of this review, no identification theory for stochastic interventions or modified treatment policies over a text-valued action space. The two published escape routes from point-treatment positivity do not reach here:

- LMTP (Diaz, Williams, Hoffman, Schenck, JASA 118(542):846-857) does not identify the static estimand when positivity fails; it changes the estimand, and its Assumption 1 is a support-preservation condition on the shift function d that the analyst must enforce by construction. What does "d maps an observed (prompt, history) pair to another pair in the support of the observed data" mean when the action is a string? The paper owes an answer and gives none. The price is also unstated: identification of natural-value-dependent policies requires the STRONG sequential randomization condition (no unmeasured common causes of A_t and all *future* actions as well as future covariates), and for some shift functions the parameter is not pathwise differentiable, so no sqrt-n estimator exists. Note also that the JASA paper covers policies depending on the natural value at time t only; a multi-round policy depends on the action history, which needs Diaz, Williams, Morzywolek, Rudolph (arXiv:2605.24167).
- Kennedy's incremental propensity score interventions (JASA 114(526):645-656) genuinely dispense with positivity, but the treatment is binary at every time point. Citing it for a language-valued action would be a misuse.
- The only infinite-dimensional precedent, Barnard, Huling, Wolfson (arXiv:2606.27518), perturbs a function-valued treatment along a single analyst-chosen basis function. That construction is parasitic on linear structure that strings do not have.

Meanwhile every estimator the paper borrows is finite-action in practice: DeepBlip's overlap assumption is written in discrete form (Pr(A_t=a|H_t)>0 for all a in A) and all its experiments are binary; the DRQ-learner's "discrete or continuous" generality is about STATE spaces, while R[pi_e] is a sum over a in A, the nuisances use action propensities and a Dirac delta(A'=a), and both environments are finite-action; Causal Transformer and CRN are categorical. Nothing in this line handles continuous, let alone language-valued, treatments. So: what is the generalized propensity over strings, what is the overlap condition, and what positivity do you claim? Without answers the blip and Q quantities are not estimands, they are outputs.

=== 4. The nuisance construction is very likely biased by the paper's own design ===

If the history or the candidate prompt is adjusted for via an embedding, Feldman, Venugopal, Spiess, Feder (arXiv:2602.15730) characterize exactly the induced bias: text conflates treatment and covariate information, so adjusting on the text representation adjusts on the treatment, and the fix is covariate residualization. In a multi-round setting the conversation history literally contains the prior treatments, so an unresidualized history embedding is simultaneously a confounder proxy and a post-treatment variable. This is not a hypothetical: it is the citable, published critique of CPO (arXiv:2602.01711), which runs DML on prompt and query embeddings jointly, and the paper under review appears to repeat it one horizon deeper. Zhong, Keith, Field (arXiv:2609.01322, EMNLP 2026) is the practical counterpart and shows the richness/overlap tradeoff is binding in finite samples.

Compounding: DeepBlip's own Appendix C error-propagation bound grows like (1+C)^{tau-k}, i.e. accuracy degrades exponentially backwards along the horizon when overlap is weak. Overlap over a language action space is, at best, unquantified. The paper's early-round blip estimates are therefore not merely unidentified but numerically hopeless, and no overlap diagnostic is reported. Ring and Schomaker (J. Causal Inference, DOI 10.1515/jci-2025-0007) exists precisely so authors can check this before fitting.

=== 5. "Train a generative prompting policy against the causal critic" is the most crowded claim of the three ===

Closest prior art, which must be cited and beaten, not omitted:

- Zhang, Wang, Dhillon, "Policy Learning with a Natural Language Action Space: A Causal Approach" (arXiv:2502.17538): multi-stage decision-making in a natural-language action space, Q-learning to estimate dynamic treatment regimes, policy learned by gradient ascent on language embeddings with a decoder mapping back to coherent text. That is claims 2 and 3 of this paper, already on the record. The paper's legitimate differentiator against it is identification, which is exactly what it fails to supply.
- Kiyohara, Cao, Saito, Joachims (arXiv:2504.02646): genuinely off-policy, logged-bandit prompt selection *per user context* with a kernel-based off-policy policy gradient over a large prompt action space. Per-instance and causal, already done for T=1.
- CollabLLM (arXiv:2502.00640, ICML 2025 Outstanding Paper): multiturn-aware rewards from simulated forward rollouts used for long-horizon credit assignment on a single response, plus a 201-judge human validation. This is the model-based competitor and it validated against humans; the paper under review does not.
- FACA (arXiv:2608.17499), T2PAM/ROSA (arXiv:2509.23166), ROSA2 (arXiv:2603.01375), T-POP (arXiv:2509.24696, ICML 2026), Multi-turn RLHF (arXiv:2405.14655): per-stage pseudo-rewards, turn-level adaptation, and Nash-convergent multi-turn preference optimization respectively.

And the decisive empirical point: Liu, Xiong, Zhang, Tang (arXiv:2606.05558) supply *exact* per-token behavior log-probabilities to IS/WIS/DR baselines for LLM-agent OPE and find they still lose badly to a learned world model, because per-token ratios over a multi-turn, vocabulary-scale action space degenerate. So even in the best case for importance-weighted causal critics, the model-based alternative wins. The paper reports no world-model or direct-method comparator, so it has not shown its critic is the right instrument, only that it is a causal-looking one.

Finally, Frauen, Melnychuk, Schweisthal, van der Schaar, Feuerriegel (arXiv:2505.13092, NeurIPS 2025) prove that a CATE-optimal second stage can be decision-suboptimal once the policy class is restricted. A generative LM policy is a restricted class. Training a policy against an effect-estimating critic is, by that paper's argument, plausibly the wrong objective — and since that result is static and binary, the paper would have to re-derive the sequential analogue rather than inherit it.

=== 6. The experiments, as described, cannot support the conclusion ===

Three mandatory controls appear absent.

- Budget-matched self-consistency. Huang et al., ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2310.01798) show intrinsic multi-round revision degrades monotonically without oracle stopping (GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0; Llama-2-70b 62.0 -> 43.5 -> 36.5) and that debate loses to plain majority voting at equal cost with the gap widening (83.0 vs 88.2 at nine responses). A multi-round policy benchmarked against single-pass CoT is benchmarked against nothing.
- A zero-information feedback control. UFO (arXiv:2507.14295) gets up to ~14% from a content-free "Let's try again," and Progressive-Hint Prompting (arXiv:2304.09797) gains from answer-conditioned re-prompting with no critic at all. Any gain attributed to the estimated blip/Q signal must exceed these.
- A critique-content ablation. Stechly, Marquez, Kambhampati (arXiv:2310.12397) find the correctness and content of the critique is largely irrelevant to iterative-prompting gains. Substituting random or adversarial critic outputs is the minimum test that the causal signal carries information rather than merely inducing resampling. Kamoi et al. (TACL 2024, arXiv:2406.01297) give the fair-comparison checklist; the submission does not satisfy it.

Also: is stopping decided using ground truth? If yes, the result is void — that single confound flips Huang et al.'s own numbers from negative to positive.

=== 7. If the counterpart is a simulated user, the estimand is the simulator's, not a human's ===

Seshadri et al. (arXiv:2601.17087, ACL 2026) find agent success swings up to 9 points purely on which LLM plays the user, with systematic miscalibration and subgroup-dependent error (worse for AAVE and Indian English speakers). Zhou et al. (arXiv:2603.11245, COLM 2026) replicate the full tau-bench protocol with 451 humans and find simulators excessively cooperative, essentially never producing realistic frustration or ambiguity, and giving uniformly more positive feedback than humans — i.e. simulator-derived rewards are biased upward, and model capability does not predict simulation faithfulness. A blip/Q critic fit on simulated interaction estimates the simulator's response function. The simulator is an unmeasured nuisance parameter that shifts the estimand, not an implementation detail, and the paper treats it as the latter.

Relatedly, sequential ignorability against a human counterpart is asserted, not argued. Unmeasured, time-varying user state — intent drift, fatigue, accumulated frustration — is a common cause of the assistant's next message and of all downstream outcomes. Absent deployment-time randomization with logged propensities, this assumption is not merely untestable, it is implausible. The one paper that tried OPE on real multi-turn LLM logs (arXiv:2510.17173) had to *reconstruct* propensities with calibrated classifiers and flags this as a bias source, on N=7 users.

=== 8. Citation hygiene ===

The reviewer should verify the bibliography end to end. Common defects in this exact literature: a nonexistent arcxiv.org host on an otherwise real citation; the broken Robins 1994 SNMM DOI 10.1080/03610928408831393 (correct: 10.1080/03610929408831393); ROSA2 (arXiv:2603.01375) cited as ICML 2026 on the strength of an author homepage with no proceedings or venue field; ProRefine cited as NeurIPS 2025 when it is a workshop paper; Progressive-Hint Prompting cited as ICML when it is the AI4MATH workshop; TextGrad cited as arXiv when the canonical citation is Nature 639:609-616 (2025); and Self-Refine's ~20% headline cited in support of a reasoning claim when its own GSM8K rows are +0.0/+0.2. Any of these is a small hit; several together undermine the "first" claim by demonstrating the literature was not actually read.

=== Summary ===

Strip the three novelty claims and what remains is: a known framing (AAAI-25, KDD 2026), two off-the-shelf orthogonal estimators (ICML 2026, ICLR 2026) applied to an action space neither supports, an identification gap the paper names but does not close, a nuisance construction that a published result says is biased, a policy-training objective a NeurIPS 2025 paper says may be the wrong one, and an evaluation missing the three controls this subfield has established as mandatory. The genuinely open problem — what positivity, support preservation, and a generalized propensity mean when the action is a string — is the paper's stated contribution and its largest omission.

=== Reframing that would survive this review ===

See the surviving_reframing field. Briefly: drop "first," drop language-valued identification, and make the contribution the *coarsening plus the instrument* — a prospectively randomized, propensity-logged multi-round deployment over a small finite set of analyst-specified prompt-move types, with residualized history nuisances, round-specific blip/Q estimates used only to decide *when* to intervene, and honest negative results against the matched-budget and zero-information controls. That I would send to reviewers.
strongest_attacks: "First to formulate" is defeated three times over, twice by peer-reviewed work the paper does not cite: Wang et al. AAAI-25 (instructions-as-treatment, verbatim in the abstract) and Frauen et al. arXiv:2605.25998 (KDD 2026), which states the prompt-as-treatment framing outright, names doubly-robust/orthogonal policy learning as the relevant tooling, and explicitly frames agentic systems as sequential decisions with causal estimands.

Longitudinal causal inference over text is already done: Nakamura and Imai arXiv:2605.07834 estimates effects of sequences of treatment features with a marginal structural model, per-feature deconfounder and semiparametric CIs, and Imai and Nakamura arXiv:2410.00903 supplies the nonparametric identification and DML asymptotics the paper lacks. Neither is engaged.

Claim 2 plus claim 3 is substantially Zhang, Wang, Dhillon arXiv:2502.17538: Q-learning for dynamic treatment regimes in a natural-language action space with a policy learned by gradient ascent on embeddings and decoded back to text. The paper's only honest differentiator over it is identification, which is precisely what it fails to provide.

The estimators are off-the-shelf. DeepBlip (arXiv:2511.14545, ICML 2026) already learns all blip functions jointly under a Neyman-orthogonal loss; the DRQ-learner (arXiv:2509.26429, ICLR 2026) is already doubly robust, Neyman-orthogonal and quasi-oracle for Q from logged trajectories. The residual contribution is the text action space, which is exactly what neither supports.

No identification theory exists for stochastic interventions or modified treatment policies over a text action space, and the paper does not supply one. LMTP (Diaz et al., JASA 118(542):846-857) only changes the estimand under a support-preservation condition the analyst must enforce by construction (undefined for strings), and charges STRONG sequential randomization plus, for some shift functions, loss of pathwise differentiability. Kennedy's IPSIs (JASA 114(526):645-656) are binary-only. Barnard et al. arXiv:2606.27518 reaches infinite dimensions only via linear basis structure text lacks.

Every borrowed estimator is finite-action in practice: DeepBlip's overlap is written discretely and all its experiments are binary; the DRQ-learner's discrete-or-continuous generality is about STATE spaces while R[pi_e] sums over a in A with action propensities and a Dirac delta; CT and CRN are categorical. So what is the generalized propensity over strings, and what overlap condition is claimed?

"Blip/Q" conflates a history-conditional contrast against a reference level 0 with a level under a fixed evaluation policy in a time-invariant Markov state. There is no canonical zero utterance in a conversation, so the blip decomposition is arbitrary-reference-dependent; and invoking Q imports a Markov assumption that assumes away the history-dependent confounding the paper claims to model.

The nuisance construction is biased by the paper's own design: Feldman, Venugopal, Spiess, Feder arXiv:2602.15730 show adjusting on a text representation adjusts on the treatment and prescribe covariate residualization. A multi-round history embedding literally contains prior treatments, so it is simultaneously confounder proxy and post-treatment variable. This is the published critique of CPO (arXiv:2602.01711) repeated one horizon deeper.

DeepBlip's own (1+C)^{tau-k} backward error-propagation bound means early-round estimates degrade exponentially when overlap is weak, and overlap over a language action space is unquantified. No overlap diagnostic is reported, though Ring and Schomaker (DOI 10.1515/jci-2025-0007) exists for exactly this check.

Even with exact per-token behavior log-probabilities, Liu et al. arXiv:2606.05558 find IS/WIS/DR lose badly to a learned world model for LLM-agent OPE because per-token ratios over a multi-turn, vocabulary-scale action space degenerate. No world-model or direct-method comparator is reported, so the causal critic is not shown to be the right instrument.

Training a generative policy against an effect-estimating critic may be the wrong objective: Frauen et al. arXiv:2505.13092 (NeurIPS 2025) prove a CATE-optimal second stage can be decision-suboptimal under a restricted policy class, and a generative LM policy is restricted. Since that result is static and binary, the sequential analogue must be re-derived, not inherited.

The evaluation is missing the three controls this subfield treats as mandatory: budget-matched self-consistency (Huang et al., ICLR 2024, where multi-round revision degrades monotonically and debate loses to majority voting at equal cost, with the gap widening), a zero-information feedback control (UFO arXiv:2507.14295 gets ~14% from a content-free "try again"; Progressive-Hint Prompting gains with no critic), and a critique-content ablation (Stechly et al. arXiv:2310.12397 find critique content largely irrelevant). Also: if ground truth decides when the loop stops, the result is void.

If the counterpart is simulated, the critic estimates the simulator's response function, not a human's. Seshadri et al. arXiv:2601.17087 (ACL 2026) find up to 9-point swings from simulator choice with subgroup-dependent miscalibration; Zhou et al. arXiv:2603.11245 (COLM 2026), replicating the protocol with 451 humans, find simulators excessively cooperative and uniformly more positive, i.e. upward-biased rewards. CollabLLM (ICML 2025 Outstanding Paper) ran a 201-judge human validation; this paper does not.

Sequential ignorability against a human counterpart is asserted, not argued. Unmeasured time-varying user state (intent drift, fatigue, frustration) is a common cause of the next assistant message and all downstream outcomes. The only real-log multi-turn LLM OPE attempt (arXiv:2510.17173) had to reconstruct propensities with calibrated classifiers on N=7 users and flags this as a bias source.

Per-instance and causal prompt selection is already published for T=1: Kiyohara, Cao, Saito, Joachims arXiv:2504.02646 does off-policy policy-gradient prompt selection per user context from logged bandit feedback, and TextGrad's instance-optimization mode already optimizes a per-instance object at test time. "Per-instance" carries no novelty; only the sequential-with-identification conjunction could.

Bibliography hygiene undercuts the "first" claim by showing the literature was not read: watch for a nonexistent arcxiv.org host, the broken Robins 1994 SNMM DOI (…928… for …929…), ROSA2 cited as ICML 2026 on author-homepage evidence alone, ProRefine and Progressive-Hint Prompting cited as main-conference when both are workshop papers, TextGrad cited as arXiv rather than Nature 639:609-616, and Self-Refine's ~20% cited for a reasoning claim when its own GSM8K rows are +0.0/+0.2.
surviving_reframing:
Drop all three "first" claims and drop the pretence of identifying effects of language-valued interventions. What survives my own attack is a much smaller paper whose contribution is a measurement instrument plus a coarsening-as-identification argument, not a framing and not an estimator.

Concretely: (1) Define the round-t action not as the emitted string but as a small, finite, analyst-specified set of prompt-move types — a factorized decision head in the spirit of the Tool/Style heads of arXiv:2510.17173 (e.g. ask-clarifying-question / decompose / request-verification / restate / no-move). The coarsening is the technical content, not a compromise: it is the measurable function of the string that makes the generalized propensity well defined, restores a checkable positivity condition, and gives the blip decomposition a non-arbitrary reference level (no-move). State it as such, and state plainly that effects of the underlying string are NOT identified. (2) Randomize that head prospectively at deployment and LOG the propensities, designing the randomization for OPE error rather than accepting whatever the deployment gives you (arXiv:2605.15108). This is the one thing nobody in this literature has: arXiv:2510.17173 had to reconstruct propensities post hoc on N=7 users; arXiv:2606.05558 calls exact propensities privileged and unavailable in deployment; CollabLLM, FACA, ROSA and T-POP are all on-policy with no propensities at all. (3) Estimate round-specific effects with the existing orthogonal machinery, cited as such — DeepBlip for blips, the DRQ-learner for Q — with history nuisances residualized per Feldman et al. (arXiv:2602.15730), aggregation at turn level rather than token level (the geometric-mean ratio of arXiv:2511.20718), and reported overlap diagnostics plus a sensitivity analysis over the reference move. (4) Use the estimated effects for one narrow, empirically checkable purpose: deciding WHEN to intervene — an uncertainty- or position-gated policy over the finite move set — rather than generating the next string. This is the only place the evidence says an effect estimate can pay: Tyen et al. show repair is competent once localization is given, and arXiv:2601.00514 finds triggering revision specifically at high model uncertainty reliably helps. (5) Evaluate against budget-matched self-consistency, the UFO zero-information control, answer-conditioned re-prompting, and a critique-content ablation with randomized or adversarial critic outputs, on real human counterparts (or, if simulated, with the User-Sim Index of arXiv:2603.11245 reported and the simulator treated as a named nuisance with sensitivity across simulator choices per arXiv:2601.17087). Report the negative results.

The honest claim is then: "the first prospectively randomized, propensity-logged multi-round human-LLM deployment with turn-level outcomes, a coarsened-action positivity argument that makes round-specific blip/Q estimands well defined over text, residualized history nuisances, and an uncertainty-gated intervention policy that beats matched-budget self-consistency and a zero-information feedback control." That is a dataset-plus-identification-argument-plus-honest-benchmark paper. It concedes the framing to AAAI-25 and KDD 2026, the sequential-text estimation to Nakamura and Imai, the language-action DTR to Zhang et al., the estimators to DeepBlip and the DRQ-learner, and per-instance causal prompt selection to Kiyohara et al. — and its remaining novelty is real, because arXiv:2605.25998 explicitly leaves the sequential/agentic case open, arXiv:2605.07834 is sequential within a document rather than against a responding counterpart, and no one has logged propensities in a multi-turn LLM deployment. I would not reject that paper.
